new_statements.quote: CN is a three-register language: it lexically contrasts high (H), mid (M), and low (L) tones which stand, each to the next, in a single melodic step relationship. [p. 26] [...] It should nevertheless be clear from these indications that relative "weight" of canonic forms is used in CN in a way similar to stress in some toneless languages: the "heavier" forms such as CVCCV and CVVN are reserved for the major lexical categories and items assimilated thereto and hence signal independent terms; while the "lightest" forms, CV, N, V, are restricted to grammatical modifiers or function words and signal dependency with respect to some other term. [p. 19]
new_statements.citation: Boyd, Raymond. n.d. [PDF dated April 2016]. The phonology and tonology of Chamba Daka (Sámá Mūm). Ms., Laboratoire Ligérien de Linguistique, Université d'Orléans. 45 pp. https://www.rblanguesdafrique.info/
new_statements.locator: III. Tonology, §1.1, p. 26 (tone statement); I. Canonic form, §3, p. 19 (stress analogy)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (45 pp., A4, Word-2007 PDF, CreationDate 2016-04-03, author RAYMOND BOYD; text layer present, extracted text used, no scanned). Both quoted passages are there verbatim at the stated locators (only straight vs curly quotation marks differ): p. 26, section 'III. TONOLOGY' §1.1 opens 'CN is a three-register language: it lexically contrasts high (H), mid (M), and low (L) tones which stand, each to the next, in a single melodic step relationship.' and goes on to list the tone-bearing units (vowels, initial syllabic nasals, nasal verb suffixes), contours HM/HL/ML/LH/LM/LHL and downstep; p. 19, §3 of part I (canonic forms) contains 'It should nevertheless be clear from these indications tha…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chamba Daka (Nnakennyaare dialect) is a three-tone language (H, M, L, plus contours and downstep) with lexical tone on every vowel; the description contains no rule for word-stress placement. Its only reference to stress is an analogy: the syllable-weight of canonic forms does the lexical-vs-grammatical signalling job that stress does in 'toneless' languages, implying CN is not such a language and does not use stress for it. No explicit claim that stress is absent or where it would fall.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonally: HM and LH contours have special realisations; LHL contour rare and merging with HL (fn. 63).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical description (uninflected base forms of nominals and verbs, citation forms); tone sandhi and utterance-final effects treated separately. The 'stress' passage concerns canonic-form weight, not prominence placement, so this is a tone-language entry without a stress rule, not a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 samb1311 'Sama Mum' = Chamba Daka / Samba Daka (ISO ccg); Raymond Boyd's site (rblanguesdafrique.info/) gives the autonym sámá mūm with ISO ccg and Glottocode samb1311 explicitly. Boyd's phonology describes the Nnakennyaare dialect of Ganye, Adamawa State, Nigeria (the lingua-franca dialect); Mapeo, Jangani, Lamja and Dirim varieties are not covered by the opened statement. Glottolog's second listed reference (Frewen 1877/78, 'Daka... on the Zambesi') is a misattribution to a Zambezi language.

sources.locator: III. Tonology, §1.1, p. 26 (tone statement); I. Canonic form, §3, p. 19 (stress analogy)
sources.note: Full phonology + tonology of the Nnakennyaare dialect. III Tonology 1.1 (p. 26): three-register tone language (H, M, L; contours HM, HL, ML, LH, LM, LHL; downstep). The only mention of stress is an analogy on p. 19: relative 'weight' of canonic forms 'is used in CN in a way similar to stress in some toneless languages' (heavy CVCCV/CVVN = lexical words, light CV/N/V = function words). No statement on stress placement or existence in CN itself.
